performers: Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Frederick Stock; Walter P. Zimmerman, organ
recorded: 22 December 1926, Orchestra Hall, Chicago; issued by Victor in July 1927
intro: Frederick Stock conducts the Chicago Symphony with Walter P. Zimmerman at the organ. Elgar saves the organ for the great return of the trio tune, when the march opens out into ceremony.

sections.label: Intro · An off-beat shout
sections.mNote: A forceful opening in E♭ before D major settles

sections.label: A · Strings begin the quick march
B · The trio in G major
sections.mNote: Violins, clarinets and horns carry the quiet tune

sections.label: A′ · The quick march returns
sections.mNote: D major and the short string phrases return

sections.label: B′ · D major, with organ
sections.mNote: Deep organ pedals support the returning trio

sections.label: Coda · The march takes its leave
sections.mNote: Running strings and short wind phrases close the march

cues.title: Zimmerman at the organ
cues.text: On 22 December 1926, Frederick Stock and the Chicago Symphony assemble in Orchestra Hall with organist Walter P. Zimmerman. Victor records four takes of the march. The third becomes the issued record.
cues.evidence: Victor recording ledger, matrix CVE-37282, reproduced by the Discography of American Historical Recordings: personnel, venue, four takes and take 3 as master. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800011535

cues.title: Accents and running strings
cues.text: The strings put two firm accents beside a quick flurry of notes. The bass answers with its own insistent figure, sometimes rubbing against the tune above it. This is the march’s busy D-major music, marked Allegro, con molto fuoco.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal A, p. 130 in this reprint: string melody and bass figure. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6e/IMSLP24159-PMLP23738-Elgar_-_Pomp_and_Circumstance%2C_Op._39%2C_No._1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horns inside the melody
cues.text: The first trio is in G major. Four horns blend with the first violins and clarinets in the long tune, while the bassoons and lower strings keep the accompaniment stepping evenly. Elgar marks the melody legato e cantabile: joined and singing.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal I, Trio, p. 138 in the linked reprint: first violins, two clarinets and four horns share the melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chicago hears it first
cues.text: Chicago has a history with this march. On 28 November 1902, Theodore Thomas conducts its American première at the Auditorium. Nearly a quarter-century later, Stock takes the same orchestra into the recording session heard here.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society dates the US première to 28 November 1902, with Theodore Thomas and the Chicago Orchestra: https://www.elgar.org/3pomp-b.htm. Stock’s 1926 session is documented in DAHR matrix CVE-37282.

cues.title: The organ’s deep pedals
cues.text: The trio returns in D major, marked Molto maestoso. Elgar brings in the organ on pedals alone, specifying sixteen- and thirty-two-foot stops. Zimmerman’s hands join later, adding chords as the tune continues to rise.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, after rehearsal R and at S. The organ part specifies pedals only, 16 and 32 feet, before the manuals enter: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e7/IMSLP50146-PMLP23738-Elgar-PompCirc1.Organ.pdf. DAHR identifies Zimmerman.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quick final flourish
cues.text: After the great tune, Elgar returns to quick notes. The strings run, woodwinds exchange short phrases, and the march ends with a clipped accent and a held D. The organ pedals join the final chord.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal T to the end, pp. 153–154 in the linked reprint; organ part, final pedal note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
